summary: Source-anchored research for Destination right-sizing after cutover. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Destination right-sizing can include choosing a simpler topology during migration: MongoDB's live-migration configuration table includes sharded-to-replica-set migration, and Percona's ClusterSync presentation explicitly describes that path as right-sizing when sharding is no longer necessary. This is a migration-plan option, not evidence that an existing sharded destination can be converted merely by lowering its instance tier after cutover. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-10)

For Atlas Core, storage auto-scaling increases capacity only; storage reduction is manual. Atlas can refuse a compute downgrade when the target tier cannot support the existing disk capacity or provisioned IOPS. Therefore, removing migration load does not by itself guarantee that the destination will return to a cheaper tier. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

A January 2024 Atlas user reported that reducing logical data to roughly 200 GB left about 900 GB of storage and prevented an NVMe M60-to-M50 downgrade. This is a historical user report illustrating a storage-related downsizing obstacle, not a verified current product-wide limitation or a measured migration outcome. (low confidence)

Atlas Core refuses automatic compute downscaling when the target tier cannot support existing disk capacity or provisioned IOPS. Depending on the current and maximum tier, Atlas can disable downward auto-scaling or raise the minimum tier. Low CPU utilization alone therefore does not guarantee a lower tier. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Size the steady-state destination from measured resource use and peak headroom, rather than copying source allocations or using CPU alone. MongoDB recommends monitoring CPU, WiredTiger cache, memory and IOPS; Microsoft's migration-sizing method independently uses CPU/memory, disk IOPS/throughput, performance percentiles and a comfort factor. Applying that general measurement method after MongoDB cutover is a synthesis, not an Atlas-specific Microsoft recommendation. (high confidence)

A defensible post-cutover sizing review uses observed workload demand rather than copying source allocations. MongoDB recommends reviewing CPU, WiredTiger cache, memory and IOPS over a rolling 30 days of normal use; Azure Migrate independently recommends performance-based target sizing using CPU, memory, disk IOPS and throughput. Applying the Azure method to Atlas is a methodological analogy, not an Atlas compatibility claim. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

For Atlas pull live migration, MongoDB permits temporarily increasing the destination cluster size during migration and recommends post-migration performance tuning and sizing to minimize costs. Its general cost guidance also recommends downsizing persistently underutilized clusters. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

MongoDB's cost-saving guide recommends a rolling 30-day period of normal use for manual downsizing analysis. That is an observation recommendation, not a mandatory 30-day wait after every cutover; the reviewed migration guidance gives no fixed post-cutover waiting period. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

MongoDB's storage documentation says Atlas works around cloud-provider restrictions on in-place disk shrinking by provisioning replacement volumes and synchronizing data; it describes downtime on each node during synchronization. Treat shrinking excess migration storage as a planned rolling operation, without inferring that every application suffers a full-cluster outage. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Migration-time compute allocation should not automatically become the permanent cost baseline: compare representative production demand with the destination tier after cutover. This is an inference from MongoDB's temporary migration sizing guidance and its recommendation to downsize consistently underutilized clusters; these sources do not establish a universal percentage saving. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

On Atlas Core, storage auto-scaling increases capacity only; reducing disk capacity requires a manual edit. Do not assume enabling auto-scaling will reverse migration-time disk growth after cutover. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

For AWS-backed Atlas storage, a capacity decrease provisions new volumes and synchronizes data to them, with downtime on each affected node. It is not an in-place disk shrink. This statement does not imply that the entire replica set is unavailable throughout the operation. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

IBM Cloud Databases for MongoDB does not permit storage downscaling; its documented route after data reduction is backup and restore to a new deployment. This is an IBM destination constraint and must not be generalized to Atlas. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

In Azure Migrate, performance-based assessments can use performance history, a chosen utilization percentile and a comfort factor to add safety headroom. This supports a demand-plus-headroom assessment method, but it does not demonstrate a MongoDB post-cutover outcome or prescribe Atlas tier settings. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-10-07)
